texto:
Amazon today said it is hiring more than 300,000 people for seasonal, part-time and full-time roles across its US core operations network for the 2026 holiday season, and that from January 1, 2027, eligible seasonal employees will receive healthcare coverage from their first day of work. The figure is 50,000 above the 250,000 target the company set for each of the previous three holiday seasons, according to press coverage of the 2025 drive, though Amazon's release does not make that comparison itself and does not say how many of the 300,000 roles are seasonal.
In Short
Amazon is hiring more than 300,000 people in the United States to pack and move orders during the busy holiday shopping months, which is more than in recent years. This matters to anyone selling on Amazon or competing with it, because the size of that workforce shapes how fast parcels arrive during Black Friday, Cyber Monday and December. Starting in January 2027, seasonal workers on at least 30 hours a week also get health insurance from their first day, something Amazon previously reserved for regular full-time staff.
What Amazon said
The announcement went out on Business Wire at 2:31 p.m. Eastern Daylight Time on October 20, 2026, datelined Seattle. It pairs a short release with a blog post by J. Ofori Agboka, Vice President of People Experience and Technology, Global Operations, at Amazon, which the company also published on its own news site.
The headline number is "over 300,000 people for seasonal, part-time, and full-time roles across its U.S. core operations network nationwide this holiday season," according to Amazon. New openings will be posted weekly from October through December. Applicants can sign up for job alerts at amazon.com/localjobs or by texting NEWJOB to 31432.
"Our seasonal roles can fill quickly," Agboka wrote. That line, a recruiting prompt, also hints at the competition for warehouse and delivery labor in the fourth quarter, when retailers, parcel carriers and logistics firms draw on the same pool of temporary workers.
Pay figures in the release are as follows, according to Amazon:
- Seasonal employees earn an average of $20 an hour.
- Full-time core operations employees start at a minimum of $20 an hour.
- Average hourly pay reaches nearly $24 an hour.
- Average total compensation, once benefits are counted, exceeds $32 an hour.
Healthcare from the first day
The most concrete policy change is about health insurance. Amazon has offered coverage from the first day to regular full-time employees "for several years," according to Agboka. From January 1, 2027, the company extends that to seasonal employees who work at least 30 hours per week.
The mechanics differ depending on start date. Eligible seasonal staff hired before January 1 gain access to coverage on January 1 itself, while those hired on or after that date are covered from their very first day. Plans start at $5 a week with $5 copays, according to Amazon.
That timing matters for the 2026 peak. A seasonal worker who joins in November and leaves before the end of December would never reach January 1, and so would not benefit from the change during this holiday season. The policy applies fully to seasonal hiring that takes place in 2027 and later, including outside the holidays, since Amazon says it "hire[s] seasonal employees year-round."
"It's rare for companies in our industry to offer healthcare starting on the first day on the job," Agboka wrote, describing the benefit as "industry-leading." The release offers no comparison with named competitors to support that claim, and it does not state what share of seasonal workers typically work 30 hours or more a week, which determines how many people the change actually covers.
"Whether someone joins Amazon for a few months or comes to build a long-term career, we want them to have access to industry-leading benefits that support them and their families," according to Agboka.
Pay, discounts and banking
Most of the pay and benefit figures in the release are not new. They restate what Amazon announced on September 16, 2026, when US operations workers gained a $1 raise to a $20 starting wage, alongside a claim of more than $1.5 billion in higher pay for the US core operations workforce. That earlier announcement provided no breakdown, timeframe or headcount for the $1.5 billion, and today's release adds none.
Agboka's post repeats the other benefits from September. Since earlier this month, according to Amazon, US employees have had an uncapped 10% discount on eligible groceries and everyday essentials on Amazon.com and Whole Foods Market online, and an uncapped 20% discount in Whole Foods Market stores, including the hot bar and salad bar. Those discounts stack with Prime member savings.
The second is Day 1 Financial, a banking benefit delivered through First Tech Federal Credit Union. Qualified employees, their spouses and their children can keep the membership for life, including after leaving Amazon. Access begins rolling out in late 2026 and becomes broadly available in 2027, according to Amazon. Neither the release nor the blog post says which employees qualify, or whether seasonal staff are among them.
Existing benefits listed for eligible employees include a free Prime membership, prepaid tuition through Career Choice of up to $5,250 a year, a 401(k) with company match, paid parental leave and 24/7 mental health support through Resources for Living. Again, eligibility is not broken down by employment type.
A small wording gap
The release and the blog post describe the $24 figure slightly differently. The release's opening paragraph and key takeaways attribute "average hourly pay reaching nearly $24 an hour" to full-time core operations employees. The blog body says "average hourly pay across our core operations workforce is nearly $24 an hour," which would include part-time and possibly seasonal staff. Amazon does not explain which population the figure covers, or how the $32 total compensation number was calculated.
How the figure compares
Amazon's release does not mention earlier seasonal hiring. Press coverage does. Retail Dive reported on October 17, 2025, that Amazon planned to hire up to 250,000 full-time, part-time and seasonal workers across its fulfillment and transportation network for the 2025 holidays, the third consecutive year at that target, with seasonal employees earning over $19 an hour on average.
On those numbers, the 2026 target is 20% higher, a PPC Land calculation, and average seasonal pay has moved from over $19 to $20 an hour. Two caveats apply. First, the 2025 figure was "up to" 250,000 while the 2026 figure is "over" 300,000, so one is a ceiling and the other a floor. Second, the 2025 drive was described as covering the fulfillment and transportation network, while the 2026 announcement uses the phrase "core operations network." Amazon does not say whether those describe the same set of facilities and jobs. PPC Land has not been able to confirm the scope from Amazon directly.
PPC Land also covered an earlier Amazon holiday hiring drive with a 250,000 target, a $2.2 billion pay investment, seasonal pay of at least $18 an hour and average total compensation above $29 an hour. That piece does not carry a visible date.
Context from the company's size helps. Amazon employed about 1.58 million people globally in January 2026, a figure cited in PPC Land's coverage of the September pay rise. Measured against that, the 300,000 US holiday roles equal roughly 19% of the global workforce, again a PPC Land calculation and only a rough indicator, since many seasonal workers leave in January.
The contrast with Amazon's corporate headcount is stark. The company cut about 14,000 corporate roles in October 2025 and about 16,000 more in January 2026, then eliminated fewer than 1,000 further roles, mainly in its Stores business, in early October 2026, as PPC Land reported on October 8. Hiring in operations and cutting in offices are not contradictory for a business whose warehouse and delivery volume peaks in the fourth quarter, but the two trends point in opposite directions.
What the release does not say
Several numbers that would matter to anyone tracking Amazon's holiday capacity are missing:
- Seasonal versus permanent split. The 300,000 figure combines seasonal, part-time and full-time roles. Amazon does not say how many are seasonal or how many will continue after the holidays.
- Locations and facility types. The release says "nationwide" and names no states, cities or count of sites. The only location in the blog post's imagery is a facility in Tulsa, Oklahoma.
- Job types. Roles are not broken down between fulfillment centers, sortation, delivery stations or transportation.
- Healthcare eligibility. No estimate is given of how many seasonal employees work 30 hours a week or more, or how many have stayed past January 1 in previous years.
- Retention. Agboka writes that seasonal employees each year "go on to become trainers, managers, and leaders," but gives no conversion rate from seasonal to permanent roles.
The blog version on Amazon's site adds that employees who stay three years see pay rise by an average of 17%. That figure does not appear in the Business Wire release.
Why the hiring number matters to sellers and advertisers
For PPC Land's readers, an Amazon hiring announcement is less a labor story than a capacity signal. The holiday calendar is already set. Prime Big Deal Days ran October 6-7 across 22 countries. Black Friday falls on November 27, 2026, and Cyber Monday on November 30, and the window for sellers to submit Black Friday Week and Cyber Monday deals closes today, October 20.
Inventory deadlines run close to today's announcement. Under the holiday calendar Amazon posted to Seller Central in July, peak fulfillment fees run from October 15, 2026, to January 14, 2027, adding an average of $0.32 per unit. Inbound cutoffs for the Black Friday Week and Cyber Monday event are October 14 for Amazon Warehousing and Distribution, October 21 for Fulfillment by Amazon shipments with minimal splits and October 28 for shipments with Amazon-optimized splits. Products arriving after those dates lose Prime badge eligibility for the event.
Those are the stock deadlines. The 300,000 workers are the people who process that stock once it lands, during what Amazon calls high velocity events, when traffic, orders and ad demand surge beyond normal levels. Delivery promises shown on product pages, and therefore conversion rates on sponsored listings, depend partly on how quickly orders clear warehouses and delivery stations in late November and December.
Delivery speed has been a central marketing claim for Amazon this year. In February, Amazon said it delivered more than 13 billion items same or next day to Prime members worldwide in 2025, with more than 8 billion US items arriving within 24 hours. Holding those speeds through the peak requires labor in addition to automation, and the 50,000 increase over the 2025 target suggests Amazon expects more volume, more labor-intensive volume, or a broader definition of the network. The release does not say which.
The return policy also extends the workload past the selling season. Amazon made its holiday return window an annual rule, covering purchases from November 1 to December 31 with returns accepted until January 31, 2027, and January 15 for Apple products. Returns processing in January falls after many seasonal contracts end, and after the January 1 healthcare change takes effect for those who stay.
What comes next
Amazon will report third-quarter 2026 results on Thursday, October 29, 2026, with a conference call at 2:00 p.m. Pacific Time, according to a separate notice listed on the same Business Wire page. The fourth-quarter report, which will cover the holiday period, follows in early 2027. Neither is likely to break out seasonal headcount, but operating costs in the North America segment will show how much the holiday labor push costs.
In the second quarter of 2026, Amazon reported total net sales of $200.6 billion and advertising revenue of $19.8 billion, up 26% year over year. Advertising income does not depend on warehouse labor directly, yet a large share of Amazon's ad inventory sits on product pages whose delivery dates are set by the operations network. A slower peak would show up in shopper behavior before it shows up in any earnings line.
The healthcare change is the part of today's announcement with effects beyond the 2026 season. It applies to every qualifying seasonal hire from January 1, 2027, onward, whenever in the year they join. How many people that covers depends on the 30-hour threshold, and Amazon has not published the number.

Summary
Who: Amazon, through a release and a blog post by J. Ofori Agboka, Vice President of People Experience and Technology, Global Operations. The announcement affects job seekers, current seasonal and full-time operations employees, and the sellers and advertisers who depend on Amazon's fulfillment and delivery network during the holiday peak.
What: Amazon is hiring over 300,000 people for seasonal, part-time and full-time roles in its US core operations network, up from the 250,000 target reported for 2025. Seasonal employees who work at least 30 hours a week will get healthcare coverage from their first day starting January 1, 2027, with plans from $5 a week. Pay figures of $20 average for seasonal staff, a $20 minimum for full-time staff, nearly $24 average and over $32 in total compensation repeat the September 16 pay announcement.
When: The announcement came today, October 20, 2026. Job postings run weekly from October through December, and the healthcare change takes effect on January 1, 2027.
Where: Nationwide across the US core operations network. Amazon names no states, cities or facility counts.
Why: The hiring supports Amazon's busiest period, which includes Black Friday on November 27 and Cyber Monday on November 30. The release does not say how many roles are seasonal, which facilities are hiring, or how many seasonal workers meet the 30-hour threshold for the new healthcare benefit, so the real scale of both the hiring and the benefit change cannot yet be measured.
